_note: Curated site catalog (prompt section 11.1; values from docs/research/sites.md and power-costs-outcomes.md, retrieved 2026-11-14). Frame: MOON_ME (LROC) unless noted. Sources are keys into refs.json. 10_sites.py cross-checks every site that has lrocObjectId against the LROC anthropogenic shapefile (updated 2026-08-14) and fails if a verified site moves more than 50 m, unless coordsFromShapefile is true (explicit override: the shapefile gives more decimals). Landing times are UTC; date-precision times are stored as a bare ISO date.

noLandingCheck.result: No lunar landing attempt found between 26 Oct 2026 and 14 Nov 2026. Blue Ghost Mission 2 and IM-3 are listed as slipped to 2027.

sites.name: Apollo 11 (Tranquility Base)
sites.blurb: Landed with the Sun about 10° above the horizon, inside a deliberate 5°-14° window so crater shadows showed the hazards. Also Shadowline's validation site.
sites.timeNote: Contact Light 20:17:40 UTC (GET 102:45:40); Mission Report touchdown GET 102:45:39.9, given by SP-4029 as 20:17:39 GMT.

sites.name: Apollo 12 (Oceanus Procellarum)
sites.blurb: The lowest Sun of any Apollo landing (about 5° in the ALSJ reconstruction), next to Surveyor 3.

sites.name: Apollo 14 (Fra Mauro)
sites.blurb: Crewed landing in the Fra Mauro highlands.

sites.name: Apollo 15 (Hadley-Apennine)
sites.blurb: First J-mission, landed between Hadley Rille and the Apennine mountains.

sites.name: Apollo 16 (Descartes Highlands)
sites.blurb: The only Apollo landing in the central highlands.

sites.name: Apollo 17 (Taurus-Littrow)
sites.blurb: The last crewed landing, in a valley ringed by massifs that shape its horizon.
sites.timeNote: NSSDCA gives 19:54:57; the ALSJ table gives 19:54:58.

sites.name: Surveyor 1
sites.blurb: First US soft landing on the Moon.

sites.name: Surveyor 3
sites.blurb: Apollo 12 landed 155 m away; the sandblasting it received is the basis for today's landing stand-off rules.

sites.name: Surveyor 5
sites.blurb: Robotic lander in Mare Tranquillitatis, about 25 km from Tranquility Base.

sites.name: Surveyor 6
sites.blurb: Made the first lunar 'hop', relaunching its engines to move a few metres.

sites.name: Surveyor 7 (Tycho)
sites.blurb: Landed on the north rim of Tycho, the only Surveyor in the highlands.

sites.name: Luna 9
sites.blurb: First soft landing on the Moon. Its exact position has never been located in LROC images, so this Soviet-era coordinate may be off by kilometres.

sites.name: Luna 16
sites.blurb: First robotic sample return.

sites.name: Luna 17 (Lunokhod 1 lander)
sites.blurb: Delivered Lunokhod 1, the first rover on another world.

sites.name: Lunokhod 1 (final position)
sites.blurb: Where Lunokhod 1 ended its traverse, not a landing point.

sites.name: Luna 20
sites.blurb: Highland sample return; its Soviet-era published position is 7.6 km from where LROC found it.

sites.name: Luna 21 (Lunokhod 2 lander)
sites.blurb: Delivered Lunokhod 2 into Le Monnier crater.

sites.name: Lunokhod 2 (final position)
sites.blurb: Where Lunokhod 2 ended its traverse, not a landing point.

sites.name: Luna 23

outcomeDetail.summary: Landed damaged and returned no sample.

sites.blurb: Landed damaged in Mare Crisium, about 6 km from where Luna 24 later succeeded.

sites.name: Luna 24 (Mare Crisium)
sites.blurb: Robotic sample return from an equatorial mare; the last landing for 37 years.

sites.name: Luna 25 (impact crater)

outcomeDetail.summary: Crashed during a pre-landing orbit burn: the engine fired for 127 s instead of 84 s. LROC calls this crater 'likely' Luna 25's; the intended site was about 424 km away.

sites.blurb: Russia's first lunar lander since 1976, lost before its landing attempt.

sites.name: Chang'e-3 (Mare Imbrium)
sites.blurb: China's first lunar landing, with the Yutu rover.
sites.timeNote: Xinhua: powered descent began 'about 21:00' Beijing time and touchdown came 'about 12 minutes later' (about 13:11-13:12 UTC).

sites.name: Chang'e-4 (Von Kármán crater)
sites.blurb: First landing on the far side, where Earth never rises above the horizon, so direct-to-Earth radio is impossible.

sites.name: Chang'e-5 (Oceanus Procellarum)
sites.blurb: Sample return from young mare basalts.

sites.name: Chang'e-6 (Apollo basin)
sites.blurb: First sample return from the far side.

sites.name: Beresheet (impact site)

outcomeDetail.summary: An inertial measurement unit fault, then a command sent to reset it, led to main-engine shutdown during descent.

sites.blurb: The first privately funded lunar landing attempt.

sites.name: Chandrayaan-2 Vikram (impact site)

outcomeDetail.summary: Descent-guidance failure: in the second descent phase 'the reduction in velocity was more than the designed value', so the fine-braking phase started outside its design conditions and Vikram hard-landed within 500 m of the designated site. ISRO cites neither the site nor the date.

sites.blurb: Lost in final descent near the south pole because of braking performance, not lighting or site choice.
sites.timeNote: Powered descent began 7 Sep 2019 IST (6 Sep UTC). The crash time is unsourced.

sites.name: Chandrayaan-3 (Statio Shiv Shakti)

outcomeDetail.summary: Soft-landed with the Pragyan rover. Designed for one lunar day (about 14 Earth days); the rover and lander were put to sleep on 2 and 4 Sep 2023 and never answered again.

coordsAsPublished.note: ISRO's planned prime landing site, 359 m from where Vikram actually landed

sites.blurb: Solar-powered and built for one lunar day; it went to sleep as night fell and never woke.
sites.timeNote: ISRO's pre-landing estimate: powered descent 'around 1745 Hrs. IST'. The exact touchdown time is unsourced from a primary.

sites.name: HAKUTO-R Mission 1 (probable impact)

outcomeDetail.summary: After crossing a roughly 3 km crater rim, the lander's software rejected its altitude data. A landing-site change made after critical design review had not been carried into the simulations of the navigation route.

sites.blurb: A crater rim on an unsimulated route confused the lander's altimetry: a real case of terrain on the approach path mattering.
sites.timeNote: LROC: 'moments before the touchdown on 25 April at 12:40 p.m. EDT' (16:40 UTC).

sites.name: SLIM (near Shioli crater)

outcomeDetail.summary: One main-engine nozzle separated at about 50 m altitude and the lander touched down in an unplanned attitude about 55 m from target. Its solar cells faced west, so it made no power until the Sun's direction changed; it later survived three lunar nights.

sites.blurb: A pinpoint landing in the wrong attitude: its panels faced away from the Sun until the Sun moved.

sites.name: IM-1 Odysseus (near Malapert A)

outcomeDetail.summary: The laser rangefinders could not be used because a manual safety switch had been left on, and the software patch to use NASA's NDL instead had errors. Odysseus came down fast on a 12° slope, broke at least one leg and came to rest tilted about 30°. It operated about seven Earth days, until the Sun left its one illuminated panel.

sites.blurb: Tipped over near the south pole, so a single sunlit panel set how long it could live.

sites.name: Blue Ghost Mission 1 (Mare Crisium)
sites.blurb: Landed upright and worked through a full lunar day plus about five hours into the night.

sites.name: IM-2 Athena (Mons Mouton area)

outcomeDetail.summary: Landed on its side in a shadowed crater about 20 m across, after 'noisy' laser-altimeter data may have contributed. With the Sun's direction, panel orientation and extreme cold in the crater, it could not recharge; operations ended in under 13 hours.

sites.blurb: Came down in a shadowed crater and lost power within hours: where you end up decides whether you get power.
sites.timeNote: NASA: 'approximately 11:30 a.m. March 6' with no time zone; the same release uses CST elsewhere, giving about 17:30 UTC.

sites.name: HAKUTO-R Mission 2 RESILIENCE (impact site)

outcomeDetail.summary: Hard landing: the laser rangefinder's performance deteriorated, or was lower than expected, during descent.

sites.blurb: ispace's second attempt, in Mare Frigoris.

artemisRegions._note: Nine Artemis-era candidate regions (NASA, 28 Oct 2024, 'in no priority order'); quoted on NASA's Artemis IV page as the candidate regions for the first crewed landing. NASA has never published coordinates. Each region is about 15 x 15 km, within 6° of the pole (NASA 2022). representativePoint is NOT a region centroid; the UI must label it 'approximate region reference'.
